Dd Christ the King For many people in our current secular world the supreme authority is the government. That is the highest power they acknowledge although they may not admit that openly. Some would say that Christianity is coming to an end. The venerable Archbishop Fulton Sheen famous said that it was not Christianity that was coming to an end but Christendom. Our current society, politics and culture is very much shaped by Christian principles and that may indeed be coming to an end. But that does not mean an end to the Catholic Church or Christianity. As Jesus himself told us (Matthew 28:20): “And know that I am with you always, until the end of the age." For Christians the highest power is the triune God and God Jesus told us “all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me ” by his Father (Matthew 28:18). The Church has designated the last Sunday in ordinary time as the Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe . In the past kings were instruments through which God’s promises to King David were to be fulfilled. This idea of the divine right of kings continued up until the Enlightenment and the French Revolution in 1789. Following that many monarchies were overthrown and governments, following Enlightenment principles, placed their trust in human reason. Monarchies were imperfect but since that time we have seen the failings of liberal democracies. The only source of perfection is Christ the King. In today’s world as we seek to build a society based on justice, peace and fraternity, we have to look to the witness of Christ and his teachings. removed_lines: THE WISDOM OF VIGILANCE THROUGH VIRTUE! As we draw closer to the end of the church’s calendar year, the of the readings especially the gospel will sound more eschatological (of final judgement), pr esenting different aspects of God’s judgement thereby exhorting us towards r eadiness for God’s kingdom.
Of what use is our spiritual journey if it is not geared towards a final end? – the need to be ready.
The Readings : First reading (Wis 6:12-16) from book of wisdom presents w isdom as a maiden radiant and unfading willing to encounter those who desire to know her.
Wisdom as a virtue, we must remember, is one of the greatest values in the ancient I srael, valued much than wealth and influence.
It’s believed to come from God and understood primarily as the art of living a good, virtuous life.
That’s why the five virgins in the Gospel (Mt.25:1-13) who were vigilant and did what they were expected were refer red to as “wise” virgins.

In the second reading (1 Thes 4:13-18), St Paul exhorts the Thessalonians who were expecting the imminent return of the Lord and worried about their dead relatives, to remain vigilant in their hope and not loose faith because at the coming of the Lord there wouldn’t be any difference between those dead in Christ a nd those still living and believing.
All will be taken up with to eternal life.
Take Home : We notice vigilance as a theme running through the readings.
It is w isdom in the eyes of the Lord to be ready.
To be ready in grace, in v irtue; not ready with fear of the final end/judgement. but more especially for the love of the peace and joy and serenity that comes with the presence life of God in you.
There is a joy, serenity and confidence that accompanies living a life in the Holy spirit.
We need to long for and trust in the guidance of God’s wisdom to make good choices.
Like the Psalmist today: “For you my soul is thirsting, O Lord, my God”. Prayer : Lord that we may know your wisdom to be vigilant to our Chr istian calling.
Amen. - Fr. John PARISH NEWSLET TER 8th November 2026 THIRTY SECOND SUNDAY IN ORDINARY T IME ROSARY Will be recited on Sunday evenings at 4 p.m. during the month of November in St. Coman's Cemetery.
